samples.text:
In many countries, the number of old people is increasing and there are fewer young workers. To pay for the pensions and health care of older people, some people think the government should raise the retirement age, while others believe young workers should pay more taxes. This essay will discuss both views.

On the one hand, raising the retirement age has some benefits. Today people live longer and are healthier than in the past, so many of them can continue working until 67 or 70. If they work longer, they continue to pay taxes and the government pay pensions for a shorter time. Also, older workers have a lot of experience and knowledge which is useful for companies.

On the other hand, some people think that younger people should pay higher taxes. Not all old people are able to work longer, especially people who have physical jobs like builders or farmers. It is unfair to make them to work until they are very old. Moreover, older people have worked hard for many years and paid taxes, so they deserve to rest. If young workers pay a little more tax, the government can take care of the elderly properly.

In my opinion, raising the retirement age is a better solution, but it should be flexible. Young people already have many financial problems, such as expensive housing and student loan, so higher taxes would make their life more harder. However, people with difficult physical jobs should be allowed to retire earlier.

In conclusion, both ideas have advantages and disadvantages. I believe that increasing the retirement age is more fairer for society, but the government must think about workers in different situations.
samples.why: Both views addressed and a clear opinion given · relevant ideas but general support · basic, repetitive linking · adequate vocabulary · several errors in comparatives, agreement and verb patterns that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
As life expectancy rises and birth rates fall, many countries face the challenge of supporting a growing number of retired people. Some argue that the best solution is to raise the retirement age, while others believe younger workers should pay higher taxes instead. In my opinion, gradually raising the retirement age is the fairer and more sustainable option, provided that exceptions are made for certain groups.

Supporters of higher taxes on younger workers argue that older people have earned the right to retire. Many have spent decades contributing to the economy and paying into the pension system, and they planned their lives around a particular retirement age. Moreover, not everyone is able to work into their late sixties. Those in physically demanding occupations, such as construction or nursing, may suffer from health problems that make continued employment unrealistic. For these people, a later retirement age could cause real hardship.

On the other hand, there are strong arguments for asking people to work longer. Retirement ages in many countries were set when people typically lived only a few years after leaving work, whereas today many enjoy retirements lasting two decades or more. Keeping experienced people in the workforce for longer increases tax revenue and reduces pension costs at the same time. In contrast, placing the entire burden on younger workers, who often already struggle with high housing costs and student debt, risk creating resentment between generations.

In my view, a gradual increase in the retirement age is the more balanced approach. However, it should be accompanied by flexible options, such as part-time work for older employees and earlier retirement for those whose jobs have damaged their health.

In conclusion, while higher taxes on younger people would protect current retirement plans, I believe raising the retirement age shares the cost of an ageing population more fairly across generations.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended with relevant reasoning · logical paragraphing with clear central topics · good topic vocabulary (life expectancy, tax revenue) · mostly accurate complex sentences with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Demographic change is placing growing pressure on pension and healthcare systems, as the proportion of older people rises relative to those of working age. Some believe the most effective response is to raise the retirement age, whereas others argue that younger workers should instead pay higher taxes. In my view, a gradual rise in the retirement age is the more equitable solution, although it must be implemented with sensitivity to differences between occupations.

The argument for increasing taxes on the working population rests on fairness to those approaching retirement. Many older people have contributed to the system throughout their working lives in the reasonable expectation of retiring at a particular age, and changing the rules late in their careers can seem like a breach of trust. Moreover, the capacity to keep working is unevenly distributed: an office worker may comfortably remain employed until seventy, but someone who has spent decades in manual labour may simply be physically unable to do so.

Nevertheless, relying on higher taxes carries significant drawbacks. Younger generations in many countries already face high housing costs and considerable educational debt, and increasing their tax burden further could reduce their disposable income, discourage them from starting families and deepen intergenerational resentment. Furthermore, retirement ages were often fixed when life expectancy was considerably lower; linking them to current longevity simply restores the original balance between working life and retirement. Keeping healthy, experienced people in employment for longer also benefits the economy by retaining valuable skills.

On balance, I believe that raising the retirement age gradually, with plenty of notice, distributes the cost more fairly. Crucially, such a policy should include provisions for earlier retirement in physically demanding jobs and encourage flexible arrangements such as phased or part-time retirement.

In conclusion, although asking younger workers to pay more would spare older people from working longer, a carefully managed increase in the retirement age offers a fairer and more sustainable means of supporting an ageing population.
samples.why: Both views fully explored and critically weighed · clear, qualified position · logical sequencing and seamless cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (equitable, longevity, disposable income) · wide range of structures, error-free.
